entries.title: New transit authority, new opportunity
entries.summary: <p>I pulled out my cellphone to call an Uber. I needed to go from my hotel in New York City’s Times Square to the American Museum of Natural History for a literary gala last spring. The price of the rideshare gobsmacked me. A 2-mile ride clocked in at $70. Um, no. So I did what any self-respecting urbanite would do — hiked up my floor-length dress and sauntered down the street in my Manolo Blahnik stilettos toward the subway. During the 10-minute ride, I observed men in tuxes and women in gowns, everyone en route to the same celebration.</p><p>Taking the subway made sense, even all dressed up, because of the $3 fare and efficiency of dodging traffic. Manhattan’s density, carless culture and expense foster a public transportation system truly for all the public, regardless of socioeconomic status.</p><p>One thought popped into my mind while people-watching on my NYC excursion: Chicago would never. And for oh-so-many reasons.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3e0000" name="module-3e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>As a frequent CTA user, I can’t recall ever pushing the turnstile in taffeta. Our bus and rail system isn’t as robust as NYC’s, but perhaps just as crucial as the routes is the Chicago Transit Authority’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/02/14/cta-regain-riders-trust-immigrants-research-funding-lane-bryant-murder-case-cook-states-attorney" >poor reputation</a>. The agency is a source of discontent for riders who complain about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/08/04/cta-canceled-bus-tracker-apps-ventra-transit" >ghost buses</a>, tardiness and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/1/20/23561291/cta-riders-survey-late-buses-train-weed-smell-trackingk-safety" >lack of cleanliness </a>at L stations. Even though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/08/cta-transit-crime-security-surge" target="_blank" >crime is down</a>, the perception is CTA is unsafe and unreliable. COVID-19 inflicted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/05/28/cta-state-inspector-general-audit-workers-paid-not-to-work-covid-pandemic" >financial challenges</a> and behavior I’d never seen before, such as cigarette-smoking in train cars.</p><p>We could be on the brink of change for the better.</p><p>A new day awaits our regional transit system, which can erase damage, inspire goodwill and reimagine more efficient public transportation. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/09/nita-northern-illinois-transit-authority-board-meeting-cta-metra-pace" >Northern Illinois Transit Authority</a> is now in effect, replacing the former regional system and charged with developing a unified transportation for the six-county region. By next year NITA will set a seamless regional fare policy across CTA, Metra and Pace.</p><p>Public transportation is more than getting from one destination to another. Ridership promotes walkability, and neighborhood equity addresses climate change and fosters economic development around stations. Our future is tied to better service. The best global cities boast a strong public transit. For Chicagoans and suburbanites, NITA represents a chance to be coordinated and not siloed, as we tend to be on other public goods.</p><p>I also see a chance to be bold beyond ensuring fiscal prudence. I attended NITA’s open house at Union Station earlier this month where the public used sharpies to spell out transit wishes. I saw a lot of pleas for no smoking and more reliable service. One idea suggested NITA board members and highly paid executives should use the system at least six times a week. Left unsaid was that buy-in from the top ensures investment.</p><p>Meanwhile, CTA says it wants to take a fresh look with a <a class="Link" href="https://ctabusvisionproject.com/getinvolved/#Events" target="_blank" ><u>bus vision project</u></a>. Ninety-six percent of Chicagoans live within a half-mile of a CTA bus stop. Riders can fill out an online survey or give their insights at a series of events at various public libraries. Metra, meanwhile, has a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/16/metra-shares-dream-plan-to-offer-trains-every-15-30-minutes" target="_blank" ><u>dream plan</u></a> of crosstown service, more frequent trains and connections to O’Hare Airport. Dreaming big plants the seeds for innovation.</p><p>It may seem small, but CTA’s clever social media game has stepped up — not just with travel updates — but by featuring behind-the-scenes moments from employees and pithy memes. (“If your girl travels all over the city with you, picks you up, opens the door for you, that’s not your girl, that’s a bus.”) After country music icon <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DduaUkfjAYJ/" target="_blank" ><u>Dolly Parton died, the Pink Line saluted her</u></a> by temporarily renaming the train after her and the song "9 To 5." The Green Line recently celebrated chanteuse and Chicago native <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DeMsfE5A74O/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Lalah Hathaway’s new album with a custom station and bus.</u></a> These gestures provide aesthetic appeal and counter the stinky, crime-ridden image of public transit.</p><p>NITA will have to toil for a long time to transform the regional system. It may take as long as getting the Red Line extension. Maybe by then I will feel comfortable enough to hike a formal gown to saunter down the L stairs in my stilettos.</p><p><i>Natalie Y. Moore is a senior lecturer at Northwestern University. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c00000" name="module-c00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: MAGA is wrong. The unrest in France has nothing to do with immigration.
entries.summary: <p>Polls being what they are, Republicans and their supporters must be feeling a bit like the condemned Frenchmen who rode to the guillotine during the Reign of Terror. It's fitting, then, that they are seizing on unrest in France as a desperate campaign gambit. "The Riots in France Are a Warning for America," declared the Federalist. And what is the lesson? "Mass immigration will split your country in two, and the two sides will eventually go to war."</p><p>Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, chairman of the Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Europe, had the script down pat: "They've been allowing this to happen for years and years, so they are reaping what they sowed. ... We're also trying to get a handle on our mass migration consequences, just like France should have done years ago. That's why I say this is a lesson to America. We are watching the future of America in France and the U.K., frankly."</p><p>So did Speaker Mike Johnson: "France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way."</p><p>JD Vance warned that "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-060000" name="module-060000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Naturally, President Donald Trump picked up the baton, telling reporters that the French protests were about "immigration, not schools," and posting:<br>"France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"</p><p>Back in reality, there is no evidence that the French protests and riots have anything at all to do with immigration. There has been extremist violence in France over the years, perpetrated by immigrants or children of immigrants, perhaps most famously the attack on the Paris offices of the magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2015 and the horrific Nice truck attack the following year that killed 86.</p><p>But that's not what's happening today, and no desperate eagerness by American Republicans to hijack these protests for their flailing campaigns can change that. There is no data on the ethnicity or color of the thousands of people arrested in the past week — France doesn't keep such records. Students in the Paris suburbs were protesting for weeks before the violence started. Similar protests have spread to Lyon, Marseilles, Lille, Bordeaux, and many other smaller cities and rural areas — and so did the violence. What originated with students protesting poorly equipped high schools expanded to farmers and labor unions.</p><p>Some of the rioters are dissolute young men who were itching to pick a fight with the police, but the original demonstrators were students complaining about the long-running underfunding of French schools. Others who joined are furious about the price of gasoline and diesel, and the high cost of living in general. So a more likely cause of the unrest in France isn't immigration but Trump's half-baked decision to attack Iran without buy-in from Congress. In fact, the high cost of fuel and associated inflation is causing unrest in other European countries including Italy, Portugal, Belgium and Albania. (The Albanians were already displeased by a corruption scandal linked to a resort development project by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump.)</p><p>The protests in France do bear a lesson for the United States, but it's not the one the GOP prefers. France has a weakness for <i>a la barricade</i>. Princeton's David A. Bell quotes an old saying: "While the United States has three branches of government, France has four: the executive, the legislative, the judiciary, and the street." In 2018, the country was nearly paralyzed by the <i>gilets jaunes</i> (yellow vests) protests over fuel taxes. But today's protests and riots are different. They have an end-of-an-era feel.</p><p>People are demanding better services and lower prices but are unwilling to make the trade-offs those things demand. France's finances are in terrible shape, the effect of low growth and high spending on entitlements. France has been a poor place to start a business for decades. A 2012 "millionaire's tax" failed and was abandoned. Efforts to deal with the crushing burden of pensions for the elderly — for example, Emmanuel Macron's push to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 — have been met with fierce resistance. France has been borrowing to cover its costs, but the bond markets are having their say, charging France more to borrow than Italy or Greece. France now spends more to service its debt than it spends on defense or education. And because America is stepping back from global leadership, the demands on France's budget for defense will only increase.</p><h3>Economic woes </h3><p>Lenders take account not just of a country's debt to GDP ratio but also its political stability and likelihood to repay its debts. When you look at France, you see rising support for Marine Le Pen, a right-wing extremist who is as soft on Vladimir Putin as she is tough on immigrants. But on the important matter of France's fiscal health, she makes Trumpian promises of cutting aid to immigrants while promising to reverse Macron's increase in the retirement age. Swell. No hope of economic sanity there. Over on the left, Jean-Luc Melenchon has made noises about repudiating part of France's debt, a fast road to Venezuelan-style collapse. There are more centrist candidates who offer more realistic reforms, but none seems to have political traction at this moment.</p><p>The United States is not, for a variety of reasons, in quite as bad shape economically as France, but the GOP, once supposedly the party that at least paid lip service to the problem of our national debt (are you out there, Paul Ryan?) has become utterly blithe about economic realities under Trump. Not only have his tariff and war policies raised prices, but his irresponsible tax cuts combined with ballooning spending have saddled us with unsustainable debt. Like France, we are now spending more on debt service than on defense.</p><p>Lenders, by nature or necessity an unsentimental bunch, don't seem to trust us more than they trust France to make sensible governing choices about taxes and spending. In fact, they trust us less. France is on fire, yet their 10-year bond yield only recently surpassed 5%, while as recently as last month we were being charged 5.2%. Potential lenders see a nation beclowned by repeated government shutdowns, threats to default on debt (by not raising the debt ceiling), and now in Trump 2.0, attacks on the integrity and independence of the Federal Reserve. It's impossible to say with specificity how threats to conquer Greenland, Iceland and Canada, the reality of abandoning Ukraine and sucking up to Putin, and wild swings of tariff policy play into perceptions of U.S. stability, but it can't be reassuring.</p><p>The lessons from France have nothing to do with immigration and irrepressible civil war. The primary lesson is: Don't spend more than you earn. Don't elect idiots who know little of economic reality and care less. Don't impose inflation-triggering tariffs on your allies. Don't start wars you have no idea how to win. Don't tell yourself fairy tales about immigrants causing all your problems when you fail at the most basic tasks of governing.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 5 places in Chicago you may not know were haunted
entries.summary: <p>By now, most Chicagoans know you don’t want to pick up young hitchhikers wearing a ball gown named Mary on Archer Avenue, it's best to steer clear of Bachelors Grove Cemetery in south suburban Midlothian after dark (probably during the day, too) and never, ever book a room on the 12th floor at the Congress Plaza Hotel. Unless, of course, you’re looking to be spooked, and in that case, good luck.</p><p>Chicago is one of the most haunted cities in America (currently at No. 3 on <a class="Link" href="https://www.travelandleisure.com/trip-ideas-most-haunted-cities-in-america-12120846" target="_blank" ><u>Travel & Leisure’s list</u></a>) where legendary ghost stories like Resurrection Mary run as deep as our pizza. But if you think you’ve heard them all, not so fast, says Adam Selzer. The Chicago tour guide, author and historian has been researching the city’s ghosts and ghouls for more than 20 years, writing books on infamous people and places like Graceland Cemetery, the “White City Devil” H.H. Holmes and serial killer Johann Hoch. But he’s also uncovered more underground stories, like mummies shrieking at the Field Museum and someone terrorizing the Lion House at Lincoln Park Zoo — two of the tales he shares below.</p><p>“I'm in microform rooms all the time,” Selzer said of how he finds these lesser-known stories. Libraries, universities and city records departments have become part of his ghostbusting process, where Selzer often looks for firsthand accounts and primary source data to verify or debunk what comes across his desk.</p><p>“My job is to be the historian and make sure the stories check out,” he added. “I like going around looking for ghosts too; I just don't necessarily expect them to show up. They never come when you're looking for them.”</p><p>Still, he says, “I’ve seen some weird stuff.” One instance was inside the basement of the Englewood Post Office (which was built over part of where Holmes’ infamous murder castle used to be) where Electronic Voice Phenomena (EVP) equipment picked up a recording of a little girl singing loud and clear.</p><p>There are many theories as to why Chicago is so haunted but Selzer likes to think “we’re just really good at telling the stories.”</p><p>Below, he shares five surprising tales. If you want to hear more, Selzer hosts ghost tours year-round, including during the week of Halloween; find more details at <a class="Link" href="http://adamchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>adamchicago.com</u></a>.</p><hr><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-860000" In 1986, then-bar owner Frank Hansen killed his pregnant wife, Julia, with an axe in their third-floor apartment above their Factory Ltd. bar, the Sun-Times reported at the time. She was left there for nearly a week before cops were called.</p><p>Before that, in 1968, the second floor was occupied by roommates John Parlea and Samuel Castell Jr., who got into a deadly fight over a pair of allegedly stolen pants, <a class="Link" href="https://mysteriouschicago.com/the-liars-club/" target="_blank" ><u>according to Selzer</u></a>. Illinois St.</h3><p>Many moons ago, the River North fire department was the site of the old Cook County Jail, “and between 1872 and 1927, about 100 people were hanged there,” said Selzer. “There were a lot of stories about it being haunted when the jail was still there.”</p><p>Nowadays, some firefighters have reported interesting occurrences, including hearing a male voice singing when no one was there, which Selzer believes may be one of the men who died at the jail: Carl Wanderer, the mastermind behind “The Case of the Ragged Stranger” in 1921, when he orchestrated the killing of his pregnant wife, Ruth, and fatally shot the assailant, making it look like a botched robbery.</p><p>“Right before they hanged him, Carl sang a little parlor song [‘Dear Old Pal O' Mine’] on the scaffold,” Selzer said.</p><h3>A few of Selzer’s favorite haunted intersections</h3><p>It’s not just buildings that have the stories — intersections across Chicago also are known for reported paranormal activity.</p><p><b>49th Street and Loomis:</b> The railroad tracks are supposedly haunted by a headless horseman, believed to be a cavalryman from the 1894 Pullman Strike.</p><p><b>Roosevelt Road and Michigan Avenue:</b> The southeast corner is where Abraham Lincoln’s funeral train would have pulled in during 1865 and became the site of the first Lincoln ghost stories. “They said you could see Lincoln himself dancing around the coffin with the flesh dropping off of his face,” Selzer said. “He’d been embalmed several times by the time he got here, but it's still an irresistible image.”</p><p><b>Ridge Avenue and Broadway:</b> In the 1800s, the Edgewater neighborhood was spooked by a guy in a hooded robe running around terrorizing people. Selzer talked to staff at the now-closed Hexe Haus nearby who said they still saw him roaming.</p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker doling out big bucks to help Democrats — and boost a 2028 presidential run
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is pouring millions into some of the country’s most consequential midterm races that could determine just how much President Donald Trump can accomplish in his final two years in office — efforts that will also help the governor in a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/pritzker-for-president-handicapping-the-illinois-governors-political-future" > potential 2028 presidential bid.</a></p><p>Pritzker, the billionaire heir to the Hyatt empire, is not only doling out his vast personal wealth to boost candidates in contentious races. He’s also building coalitions with Democrats across the country, including in 2028 early primary states. Beyond his own political future, a Democratic-led House or Senate would be essential for any Democratic presidential candidate to get things done in the next term.</p><p>Since 2025, Pritzker has given at least $40 million to Democrats and allied causes — including campaigns for Congress, Senate, attorney general, secretary of state, county judges, and state parties in more than a dozen states, as well as ballot fights over abortion rights and redistricting. That figure includes $15 million he contributed to his own PAC called Ready for the Fight, which is running ads in Tennessee, Arkansas, Alabama and Ohio. </p><p>"He's doing everything right. I have never met him, but he is on my list of presidential candidates. So far, in the running is [Kentucky Gov. Andy] Beshear, Pritzker, and [Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] AOC in that order," said Howard Dean, former Vermont governor, presidential candidate and chair of the DNC. "I'm impressed. More more importantly than all the giving is how he's conducted his governorship. Despite my liking AOC, I'm determined, with that exception, to elect somebody who's been a governor who's not from Washington, and he fits the bill."</p><p>Dean called Pritzker's widespread Democratic contributions "investments," saying "they're not just out of the goodness of his heart."</p><p>"It's a terrific strategy," Dean said.</p><h3>Contributions spread across the country </h3><p>Pritzker kicked off his midterm campaigning for other candidates in August, attending a get-out-the-vote canvass in Orlando with Rep. Maxwell Frost and Florida gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. He has also headlined state party dinners in Oklahoma, Texas, Georgia, Indiana, Colorado, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Arizona and Texas. And since last year, he's attended fundraisers and events in South Carolina, Washington, D.C., New York, Florida, New Hampshire, Louisiana, North Carolina, Massachusetts, Nevada, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maine, Alabama, California and New Mexico.</p><p>During a NAACP conference in South Carolina last month, Pritzker described November as "an election that will define America's next chapter.</p><p>"I'm here right now because everything we care about is under siege, and I want to be where the freedom fighters are right here," Pritzker said. "And I'm here because we're in a generational battle to preserve voting rights, and that battle is on behalf of all of the people in the Palmetto State, in the land of Lincoln, my home state, and everywhere that the embers of democracy still burn bright."</p><p>Pritzker’s largest contributions this cycle include $1.5 million to the Wisconsin Democratic Party, $1.2 million to Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor, $1 million each to the Democratic Governors Association, Senate Majority PAC, Ohio Democratic Party, the House Majority PAC and Project Battleground, a leadership committee helping Keisha Lance Bottoms' Georgia gubernatorial campaign. He also gave $310,000 to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.</p><p>State party contributions include $500,000 each to the Iowa and Michigan Democratic parties, $270,000 to the Democratic Party of New Hampshire, $150,000 to the North Carolina Democratic Party, $125,000 to the Democratic Party of Georgia, $100,000 each to the Maine, South Carolina and Texas Democratic parties. South Carolina are New Hampshire are early primary states in 2028.</p><p>Senate candidate contributions include $54,300 to Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina, $50,000 to support Minnesota Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan, $7,000 each for his running mate Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton's Senate campaign, Mary Peltola's Senate campaign in Alaska, Cooper in North Carolina and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown in Ohio. He also gave $3,500 each to Kentucky Senate candidate Charles Booker, Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, New Hampshire Senate candidate Chris Pappas and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/06/23/gov-pritzker-top-chicago-fundraiser-senate-candidate-james-talarico-texas" >Texas Senate candidate James Talarico.</a></p><div </figure> </div> </div><p>The governor also hosted Chicago fundraisers Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Talarico this year.</p><p>First Lady MK Pritzker this week said she was “fired up about MAGA men,” and donated $500,000 to Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor in Ohio. The first lady, who is also a prolific donor, also wanted a rare public statement out because she was upset about an ad Acton’s opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, ran featuring Acton’s mother, who has been estranged from Acton since her husband was indicted on a charge of raping Acton as a child.</p><p>The first lady said the race was about “standing up to bullies, confronting extremism, and making damn sure that men who thrive on cruelty and division don’t get a free pass to govern.”</p><p>Pritzker isn’t the only Illinois Democrat wading into battleground states. Stratton, who is vying for Sen. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Illinois, visited a Ohio Democrats campaign office in Akron on Oct. 22 as she stumps for Senate candidate Sherrod Brown. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided photo </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The governor's detractors are also taking notice of his focus on races outside of Illinois.</p><p>"Billionaire Governor JB Pritzker has unlimited time and money to spend on his political ambitions, while leaving Illinois in the dust," Illinois House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, said. "We need a governor committed to Illinois families, instead of mismanaging state agencies, bloating budgets and leaving the bill for future generations to pay."</p><p>The campaign for Pritzker's Republican opponent in the Nov. 3 race for Illinois governor, Darren Bailey, said Pritzker "is trying to do what he did in Illinois — buy political power. These donations are nothing but a blatant effort to build support for his delusional 2028 presidential run. JB Pritzker, foreground, speaks prior to the live broadcast of the WTTW News Gubernatorial Forum on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Renée Crown Public Media Center in Chicago. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a7ebebe/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5765x3235+0+304/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9a%2F30%2F230cd54743bc80f9f28eaa2a20e5%2Fgovdebate-261015-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd07ba0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5765x3235+0+304/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9a%2F30%2F230cd54743bc80f9f28eaa2a20e5%2Fgovdebate-261015-15.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a7ebebe/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5765x3235+0+304/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9a%2F30%2F230cd54743bc80f9f28eaa2a20e5%2Fgovdebate-261015-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Republican challenger Darren Bailey listens as Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, foreground, speaks prior to the live broadcast of the WTTW News Gubernatorial Forum Oct. 13 at the Renée Crown Public Media Center in Chicago. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>‘He doesn’t just willy-nilly’</h3><p>There is a strategy attached to Pritzker’s political giving. Beyond frequent phone calls and requests from people like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, there’s a goal of helping candidates who are perhaps being overlooked in the waning days of the election cycle — with donors moving on to more high profile or popular races. Pritzker also hopes that donations from him might signal to the donor world that they should also help the same Democrats.</p><p>The Lance Bottoms contribution came because there was a belief that coordinated campaign money was drying up — and focused on Ossoff. Pritzker wants his contributions to actually move the needle forward. He’s known to contribute to federal candidates whom he knows personally, like Hinojosa, but also those that are known to his staffers, including former Pritzker deputy campaign manager and political adviser Quentin Fulks, who ran Sen. Raphael Warnock’s reelection campaign in Georgia in 2022 and helped lead the Illinois Future PAC supporting Stratton’s Senate campaign. The governor also has a strong relationship with Texas Democrats, whom he helped during their redistricting battle last year.</p><p>Beyond Democratic leaders making fundraising requests, the requests for contributions from campaigns are constant. </p><p>“For him, he doesn't just willy-nilly. He does think through, ‘What is this money going to be used for? Will there be a strategic advantage?’” a source with direct knowledge of Pritzker’s spending said. “‘What do you need it for?’”</p>

entries.title: Review: ‘Mud Row’ at Theater Wit
entries.summary: <p>When my grandmother moved to Seattle from Texas in the 1960s, the city was redlined. There is one historic Black neighborhood in Seattle, the Central District, so, because of discriminatory housing practices, that’s where she settled. Many family members followed her; at one time, my family owned three houses in the neighborhood.</p><p>In the early 2000s, in the grips of gentrification, my aunt sold the last home our family had in the neighborhood. She made a huge profit, but it caused a deep rift in our family, and at the time I didn’t fully understand why. Today, the Central District is only around 10% Black, and after an influx of tech people found the neighborhood desirable, the values of the homes, including those purchased generations ago for tens of thousands of dollars, have skyrocketed.</p><p>The problem with selling these homes was not simply about the profit — it's about the loss of community.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Mud Row’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dc0000" name="module-dc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Nov. 15<br><b>Where:</b> Theater Wit, 1229 W. Belmont Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $38-58<br><b>Run time:</b> 90 minutes with no intermission</div> </div><p>These were my thoughts watching Dominique Morrisseau’s “Mud Row,” now at Theater Wit in a production by Remy Bumppo Theatre Company. Morrisseau's writing has a keen way of encapsulating the universal experience of Black families. Whether it’s “Detroit 67,” which also has themes of homeownership, inheritance and legacy; “Pipeline,” which made my mom cry in the theater while watching characters that reminded her of us; or “Confederates,” a story that also connects past to present by showing parallels of challenges faced by Black women in the antebellum south and a university campus in the present day — her plays, and her characters, feel so <i>real</i>.</p><p>Director Malkia Stampley worked wonders with the cast, a talented troupe that includes a stellar performance by Ayanna Bria Bakari (“Purpose” at Steppenwolf). This play has its fair share of moments where two characters are on stage, at times seated, and just talking. That’s an easy way to lose an audience. The trust Stampley had with this cast to carry those scenes made way for scathing drama, especially when Bakari was center stage with Tiffany Renee Johnson (“Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” Broadway tour). These estranged sisters are forced to find a path to reconciliation, and the road is more than a little bumpy.</p><p>“Mud Row” is set in Mud Row, a historically Black neighborhood in West Chester, Pennsylvania. Two generations of sisters are faced with navigating their own opposing personalities and ideologies, while maintaining ownership of a home passed down from their foremothers that had once been a stop on the Underground Railroad.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Alexis Janae (left) and Toccara Castleman portray sisters Elsie and Frances in “Mud Row.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Both sets of sisters have compelling stories. Elsie and Frances (played by Alexis Janae and Toccara Castleman), the elder generation, live in the neighborhood pre-Civil Rights. Frances is quick-tempered and bold. She’s a fighter, which she sees as a necessity. Whether protesting segregation or standing up to men on behalf of her sister, Frances has no backdown. Elsie, who becomes a mother and eventually passes the home, along with her strong belief of the Talented Tenth (the theory that the top 10% of Educated Blacks should lead the fight for rights, a concept popularized by W.E.B. Du Bois), down the line, is the polar opposite of her sister. Inspired by Du Bois, she believes education and an upward marriage, not violence, will lead to equality and freedom. Unfortunately for her, being born to a mother she describes as a whore, she’s uneducated. Her path leaves her jilted at the altar and forced to raise her daughter, and at times her granddaughters, on her own.</p><p>Stampley seamlessly weaves the story of Elsie and Frances into the modern-day plight of Regine and Toshi (Bakari and Johnson), Elsie’s granddaughters. At times, the characters' moments on stage melt together, and while time prohibits interacting, the ghosts of the past seemingly haunt the realities of the living. These sisters, living in the present day, have a contemporary conflict: what to do with the old house inherited from grandma, which is now worth a lot of money.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ayanna Bria Bakari and Jamaque Thomas portray married couple Regine and Davin in “Mud Row.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This is an issue I’ve witnessed tear Black families from my old neighborhood apart. Like Toshi in the play, there is too often a sibling who needs housing, while the Regines of the world are looking to cash out. Davin, Regine’s husband, played with a deft, educated-masculine air by Jamaque Thomas, provides crucial context to the dilemma through his belief of the importance of community.</p><p>The production parses these all-too-real circumstances with a dash of humor, but leans heavily on truth and strong performances from the ensemble. At a time when homelessness remains <a class="Link" href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/homelessness-declines-remains-near-record-high" target="_blank" ><u>near record levels</u></a>, and Black neighborhoods throughout the country are facing rapid gentrification, this production that originally premiered in 2019 still feels fresh.</p><p>And with none of the homes my family owned in our historically Black neighborhood reaching my generation, I found myself rooting for Regine and Toshi to hold on to theirs.</p>

entries.title: Man sexually assaults tenant at gunpoint after strangling another woman in same Chatham apartment, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 58-year-old man is being questioned by detectives Friday after his tenant reported he sexually assaulted her at gunpoint after he allegedly strangled another woman whose body lay on a couch nearby on the South Side, according to city police reports. </p><p>Police received a 911 call about 9:20 a.m. Thursday from a friend of a 28-year-old woman who reported being sexually assaulted at gunpoint by her landlord at an apartment in the 8100 block of South Ellis Avenue, according to reports from the Chicago police and the city's Office of Emergency Management and Communication (OEMC).</p><p>The 28-year-old woman said while the attack happened, she noticed another woman who "may be dead," lying on a couch, according to the reports. The 28-year-old was taken to Advocate Trinity Hospital for medical attention and a sexual assault kit.</p><p>Around the same time, the landlord, 58, walked into the Grand Crossing police station, 7040 S. Cottage Grove Ave., and "admitted to killing victim by strangulation," according to the police report. </p><p>When police conducted a well-being check at the Ellis Avenue address, they found the door locked and no one answered. Fire department crews breached the door and found the unresponsive victim, an unidentified 36-year-old woman, unclothed and covered in a sheet, on a couch in the living room, according to the report. </p><p>She was pronounced dead on the scene by the University of Chicago Medical Center according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. An autopsy is scheduled for Friday. </p><p>No charges have been announced for the 58-year-old man, who police have called a "person of interest."</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating.</p>

>Abby Miller</a></h5><p><b>Strained grid</b>: Illinois' electric grid is stressed, thanks to the demand from huge data centers rapidly multiplying to power artificial intelligence. There are more than 100 data centers in northern Illinois, each needing enough electricity to power a midsize city. Data centers require every bit of electricity that Illinois power sources — nuclear, coal, natural gas, wind and solar — can produce.</p><p><b>Why you're being billed</b>: Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydiikruy-l-e/" target="_blank" >belongs to a multistate power consortium</a> that connects us to a dozen other states across the eastern U.S., allowing states to give or take power from partners. ComEd customers are seeing higher bills, in large part because data centers are expanding everywhere. Because these data centers require enormous amounts of energy, the price of electricity is determined by the needs of this larger pool of states.</p><p><b>Estimated cost</b>: ComEd expects to spend <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydiikruy-l-s/" target="_blank" >more than $3 billion to connect data centers to its electric grid in the coming years</a>, but it has only collected about one-fourth of the costs from data center developers — a troubling gap that could leave Illinois consumers on the hook, according to consumer groups.</p><p><b>Substation pushback</b>: Beyond his own political future, a Democratic-led House or Senate would be essential for any Democratic presidential candidate to get things done next term.</p><p><b>Adding up</b>: Since 2025, Pritzker has given at least $40 million to Democrats and allied causes — including campaigns for Congress, Senate, attorney general, secretary of state, county judges, and state parties in more than a dozen states, as well as ballot fights over abortion rights and redistricting. readies its return</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydiikruy-l-it/" target="_blank" >Courtney Kueppers</a></h5><p>As the sun sets Saturday, Columbus Drive will come alive with a fire-breathing dragon, giant animal puppets, and scores of drumlines and dance troupes.</p><p>The annual Arts in the Dark parade, now in its 12th year, is not your typical parade. Instead, this night of spooky festivity is all about putting on a performance and celebrating parading as an art form, said Mark Kelly, the event's co-founder and artistic director.</p><p>This year, roughly 100 groups will bring 5,000 performers, ranging from high school marching bands to an all-woman lowrider car club. Plus, there will be giant alebrijes, a 60-foot glow worm, circus acts and ballet folklórico dancers.</p><p>It's meant to celebrate the city's diversity. Plus, for Kelly, it's a chance to embrace Halloween as an artist's holiday.</p><p>"It's the purest of all of the holidays in this country, and we're declaring it as ours. ... Arts in the Dark intends to be a celebration of the creative life of our city," Kelly said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydiikruy-l-ii/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu<br><b>Copy edited by</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Man charged with fatally beating man near Avondale railroad tracks
entries.summary: <p>A man is expected in court Friday, accused of fatally stabbing a man near railroad tracks last July in Avondale, Chicago police said.</p><p>Tomas Velasquez-Argueta, 48, was arrested Wednesday in the 1300 block of Madison Street in Evanston and charged with first degree murder, Chicago police said. </p><p>Velasquez-Argueta allegedly<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/07/08/one-dead-in-avondale-homicide" target="_blank" > fatally stabbed Juan Carlos Jaramillo</a> July 8, 2025 in the 3400 block of North Kimball Avenue, police said.</p><p>Jaramillo was found around 1:50 a.m. and pronounced dead at the scene, police said. An autopsy determined he died of multiple sharp force injuries and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Velasquez-Argueta was expected to appear in court Friday for a detention hearing. </p>

entries.title: Bulls will broadcast 20 home games in Spanish via SAP
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls will make a Spanish-language broadcast available for 20 home games this season via the SAP function, beginning with the home opener Saturday night against the Wizards.</p><p>SAP (secondary audio program) broadcasts will be available on Chicago Sports Network’s linear and app feeds, as well as on Bulls.com, which will carry only the audio. Miguel Esparza will call the action with Elio Benitez and Jorge Moreno, who will share the analyst’s chair.</p><p>The Bulls aired all 41 of their home games on Spanish-language WRTO-AM (1200) for the last three years. But the station, owned by Latino Media Network, stopped carrying them. The SAP broadcast was the team’s solution. It’s believed to be the Bulls’ first usage of SAP.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: La junta de CPS aprueba nuevo contrato que aumenta los sueldos para el personal de las cafeterías
entries.summary: <p>La Junta de Educación de Chicago aprobó el jueves un nuevo contrato con el personal de los comedores escolares después de más de un año de negociaciones, elevando los sueldos mínimos de los trabajadores y evitando una huelga.</p><p>Según el acuerdo, los trabajadores representados por el sindicato Unite Here Local 1, incluidos cocineros y asistentes, recibirán aumentos sobre su sueldo actual, así como incrementos según su puesto y antigüedad. Los sueldos fueron un tema clave para el sindicato, que ha informado que muchos de los trabajadores de las cafeterías que representa tenían dificultades para costear necesidades básicas con su último contrato.</p><p>Unite Here Local 1 representa actualmente a aproximadamente 1,500 trabajadores de comedor de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS), según el sindicato.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-830000" name="module-830000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Todo el personal de comedor ganará al menos $21 por hora bajo el nuevo acuerdo y los subgerentes podrán ganar hasta $27 por hora, según CPS. El próximo verano, todos los empleados recibirán un aumento por costo de vida del 4%, seguido de un incremento del 2.5% en 2028.</p><p>Anteriormente, una gran mayoría de los trabajadores de comedor <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/27/cps-lunchroom-workers-wages-so-low-they-can-barely-feed-own-families-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" >ganaban $18.42 o menos por hora,</a> según el sindicato. Los sueldos promedio oscilaron entre aproximadamente $23,400 y $37,400, según la nómina de empleados de CPS de principios de este año.</p><p>Una encuesta que el sindicato realizó en 2025 encontró que casi la mitad tenía problemas para pagar por sus necesidades básicas, y el 67% tuvo dificultades para pagar alimentos en ocasiones. La encuesta también halló que el 22% de los trabajadores recibía beneficios SNAP y acudía a bancos de alimentos.</p><p>Un análisis del Chicago Sun-Times a principios de este año identificó a CPS entre los 10 principales empleadores del estado en términos de número de sus trabajadores que reciben asistencia alimentaria de SNAP.</p><p>Letia Downing-Lowe, asistente de la cafetería en la primaria Eli Whitney durante 11 años, calificó el acuerdo como "un soplo de aire fresco" y dijo que los trabajadores del comedor se sienten "más respetados".</p><p>"Hemos puesto sobre la mesa mucho más de lo que no teníamos", dijo Downing-Lowe, quien también formó parte del equipo negociador del sindicato.</p><p>Los trabajadores de larga trayectoria como Downing-Lowe verán aumentos adicionales bajo el nuevo contrato. Aquellos con 10 años de servicio recibirán un aumento de $1 por hora y los que tengan 20 años verán aumentos de $2 por hora, dijo CPS.</p><p>El acuerdo también establece una estructura salarial más "consistente" para los gerentes y cocineros del comedor, según el distrito. Su sueldo antes se basaba en la cantidad de comidas servidas en la escuela.</p><p>El nuevo acuerdo cubre cuatro años, desde julio de 2025 hasta junio de 2029, y le costará al distrito casi $65 millones, dijo CPS. El distrito tendrá que realizar pagos retroactivos para cumplir con el acuerdo. El último contrato venció en junio de 2025.</p><p>Los sueldos y los niveles de personal fueron dos de los principales puntos de fricción en las negociaciones, según el sindicato. CPS <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/15/cps-will-cut-teachers-and-five-student-non-attendance-days-as-district-looks-to-close-budget-deficit" target="_blank" >ha reducido de forma constante el número de trabajadores de las cafeterías</a> mientras enfrenta déficits presupuestarios continuos.</p><p>Downing-Lowe espera que el nuevo contrato atraiga a más personal.</p><p>"Porque los sueldos han subido, con suerte podremos contratar a nuevas personas y la plantilla podrá volver a donde estaba", dijo Downing-Lowe.</p><p>El sindicato tomó medidas escalonadas en los últimos meses cuando las conversaciones parecieron estancarse y se vislumbró la posibilidad de una huelga.</p><p>En abril, miembros del sindicato <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/23/lunchroom-workers-plan-to-block-traffic-as-contract-talks-with-cps-stall" target="_blank" >llevaron a cabo actos de desobediencia civil</a> para "hacer sonar la alarma" sobre su necesidad de un nuevo contrato. Varios trabajadores fueron detenidos por la policía después de sentarse en la calle frente a la sede de CPS para llamar la atención sobre la falta de un contrato.</p><p>Ambas partes también habían acordado recurrir a un mediador federal que suele intervenir cuando las conversaciones llegan a un punto muerto para evitar una huelga.</p><p>Y en julio el sindicato solicitó el inicio de un proceso de investigación de los hechos. Ahí, una tercera parte revisa los argumentos de ambos lados de la disputa y emite un informe. Según la ley estatal, los trabajadores de los distritos escolares no pueden hacer huelga hasta 30 días después de la publicación del informe.</p><p>Pero el sindicato y CPS alcanzaron un acuerdo tentativo el 1 de octubre y fue ratificado por el sindicato el 11 de octubre, según el distrito.</p><p>En la reunión de la junta del jueves, la superintendente y directora ejecutiva de CPS, Macquiline King, celebró el acuerdo.</p><p>"Agradezco a nuestros empleados de las cafeterías por su dedicación, les doy las gracias por permanecer con nosotros y me alegra que se haya alcanzado un acuerdo que reconoce su compromiso con nuestros estudiantes y las comunidades escolares", dijo King.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Leo big man Elon Henderson among several local standouts at annual Pangos frosh/soph event
entries.summary: <p>Fresh off a season where Leo won 28 games and finished fourth in the state in Class 3A, coach Jimalle Ridley’s Lions — and promising big man Elon Henderson — will look to take another big step this season.</p><p>Everyone returns for Leo, including Henderson, a talented 6-8 sophomore. Henderson was one of the top talents on display this past weekend at the annual Pangos All-Midwest Frosh/Soph Camp held at De La Salle.</p><p>While all the pieces and production return for Ridley, it’s Henderson who is blessed with the most upside and potential impact.</p><p>“Going into the offseason, and as we have been preparing as coaches, we’ve written on the white board that the player that has to take the biggest leap in production in every single statistical category has to be Elon,” Ridley said.</p><p>His size alone will be difference-making, but at the Pangos event he displayed the strides he’s made since last season. That includes polishing up his offensive game while facing the basket.</p><p>“People would be surprised to know Elon was third on our team in made threes last season,” Ridley pointed out. “He can shoot it. He’s versatile at 6-8. He’s made a leap, though, in his facing up to the basket, playing with his chest to the rim instead of his back to the rim.”</p><p>But the area of improvement Ridley is also excited about is the work his prized sophomore has put in with his conditioning.</p><p>“His conditioning is so much better,” Ridley said. “He’s made a major leap in getting his body in much better shape. He’s stronger. He can play harder for longer stretches of time. He’s worked hard.”</p><h3><b>Pangos co-MVPs from the Catholic League</b></h3><p>A pair of young players from the Catholic League were named co-MVP of the Pangos Camp: Marist freshman Robert Smith, Jr., and De La Salle’s Zahari Threatt. Smith is a super-skilled, shot-making 6-3 freshman guard, while Threat, who opened some eyes this past summer, is a still raw but very intriguing 6-7 sophomore.</p><h3><b>Bloom’s young talent is plentiful</b></h3><p>The pool of young talent at Bloom continues to get deeper.</p><p>Sophomore guard Keiwon Gulley simply looked the part this past weekend by playing wiser and more mature than most of the other young players on display. A full season of varsity basketball will do that for you. Both Gulley and backcourt mate Kaden McClellan are seasoned sophomores.</p><p>But a pair of up-and-coming freshmen are tantalizing talents. Larry Ellis, a versatile guard with size at 6-3, and long, lanky 6-7 Louis Johnson are two of the top prospects early on in the Class of 2030.</p><h3><b>Other thoughts from Pangos </b></h3><ul id="rte-a7b6d592-cef6-11f1-b6be-137b3f58ff8d"><li>Sophomore guard TJ Jamison has garnered the most hype at Young as one of the top prospects in the Class of 2029. But another sophomore, guard Mason Spicer, is coming fast.<br></li><li>While St. Laurence has a ton of experience and perimeter firepower all lined up for what is expected to be a big season ahead, keep an eye on Bennett Meier down the road. The smooth 6-4 freshman was especially impressive this past weekend.<br></li><li>A sleeper in the Public League is Ryan Whitt of Phillips. The 6-5 sophomore is a big, bruising wing with developing ball skills and shooting on the perimeter.<br></li><li>A player to monitor this season who hasn’t received any fanfare yet — and was overlooked in selecting players for the Cream of the Crop All-Star games at Pangos — was Oak Lawn’s Dillon Matthews.<br></li><li>Another very promising group of talent waiting in the wings at Benet, headed by a trio of freshmen: 6-5 James Rydberg, 6-3 Luke Beran and 6-6 David Pauliukonis.<br></li><li>Geneva was well represented at Pangos. The Vikings should have the best backcourt in the DuKane Conference –– and it’s a young one. Heady and poised sophomore Cody Rader will pair up with another sophomore, 6-1 Jonny Udoiwood.<br></li><li>Several young players from the Public League had their moments at Pangos. The list include sophomore Kamasi Jones, a fun-to-watch 6-2 guard who transferred from DePaul Prep to Phillips, DK Heard, one of the top prospects in the sophomore class who is now at King after starting at Mount Carmel last year, and Kenwood freshman Elijah McKinnie.<br></li><li>Arguably the most impressive Illinois player from outside the Chicago area was freshman Brysen Morris of Bloomington. The 6-4 guard follows up the freshman season Dallas Marshall put together a year ago at Bloomington as he averaged 18 points a game.<br></li><li>Mamadou Baker is another out-of-the area player to watch. The 6-7 Rockford Guilford big man flashed a whole bunch of upside for just a freshman.</li></ul>

entries.title: Connor Hellebuyck trade shakes up Central Division, but Blackhawks must focus on themselves
entries.summary: <p>Of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' mere 23 regulation losses in 2016-17, one man — young Jets goalie Connor Hellebuyck — was singlehandedly responsible for four of them.</p><p>Hellebuyck stonewalled the Hawks in four consecutive meetings between November and January that season —  his first as a full-time stater — before finally letting them have one in February.</p><p>He has remained a thorn in the Hawks' side ever since, too, while establishing his reputation as arguably the NHL's best goalie. In 32 career matchups against the Hawks, he's 23-8-1 with a .921 save percentage and 2.25 goals-against average.</p><p>So the fact that Hellebuyck has now finally left the Central Division represents a small victory for the Hawks.</p><p>The Jets dealt the 33-year-old star to the Devils on Friday, ending a monthslong stalemate following his offseason trade request.</p><p>They received a respectable package in return — headlined by prospect Alexander Command and NHL center Dawson Mercer — but it's always difficult to win a trade in which you're relinquishing the best player involved. That's doubly true when you have minimal leverage.</p><p>It'll be interesting to see if this knocks over any other dominos standing around the league. Dylan Larkin, Hellebuyck's U.S. Olympic teammate, remains stuck in a similar post-trade-request stalemate with the Red Wings. Quinn Hughes, another U.S. Olympian, hasn't yet signed an extension with the Wild as his blockbuster 2027 free-agency approaches.</p><p>Plus, restricted free-agent defensemen Simon Edvinsson (Wings) and Alexander Nikishin (Hurricanes) are still holding out for richer contracts, and both seem more likely to be traded than to return to their former teams.</p><p>The Hawks probably won't get involved in any of that drama, though. Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson stuck his head out to make one major trade acquisition (Bowen Byram) this summer, but he's otherwise dedicated to letting the team's young core grow together on their own timeline.</p><p>Besides, the Hawks need to get Byram going — along with the rest of their roster — before they can think about doing any more buying.</p><p>Byram's first month in Chicago certainly hasn't gone as planned. He (understandably) missed one game for his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/05/blackhawks-bowen-byram-new-dad-stabilize-defense" >daughters’ birth</a> and has now missed three consecutive with an upper-body injury, which coach Jeff Blashill said isn't a concussion.</p><p>And in Byram's six appearances, his play has been inconsistent at best. The Hawks have been outscored 7-3 and outshot 60-43 during his five-on-five ice time. His pairing with Alex Vlasic didn't click at all, prompting a move back to his natural left side (paired with Artyom Levshunov) before his injury.</p><p>Six games don't paint a full picture, however, especially considering Byram has been adjusting to new systems, new teammates and a surely hectic home life in a new city.</p><p>There's still plenty of time for him to change the narrative and become the difference-making defenseman —perhaps even the No. 1 defenseman — the Hawks boldly proclaimed he would be.</p><p>If Byram becomes that and the rest of the Hawks start figuring things out, there's a clear path for them to climb the division hierarchy. The Jets (4-3-3), Blues (5-4-1) and Predators (3-3-3) all appear as mediocre as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/06/blackhawks-playoffs-nhl-central-division-jets-blues-predators-mammoth" >anticipated</a>. With the Pacific unsurprisingly looking like hockey's weakest division, the Central's fifth-place team should be in the wild-card conversation.</p><p>But just like with the league-wide trade chatter, the Hawks would be best served ignoring everything around them and focusing on themselves.</p><p>For as clear as the path to climb the standings appears, the path already trodden for the Hawks is the one that goes in circles around the league basement — and that's the path every prognosticator, analytic model and betting line expects them to continue following.</p><p>It will take lots of work and a little defiance to establish themselves on a different, upward trajectory, regardless of the goalies they're facing.</p>

entries.title: A jury set to decide who owns the work of Henry Darger, Chicago’s most famous outsider artist
entries.summary: <p>A federal jury is soon expected to decide who legally owns the artwork and writings of Henry Darger, more than 50 years after the death of the North Side hermit. The work is estimated to be worth millions of dollars.</p><p>This week, U.S District Court Judge Thomas Durkin set a March 8, 2027 date for a jury trial, expected to last about a week.</p><p>“A case filed in 2022 deserves to get a trial date,” Durkin told the attorneys in the case Thursday.</p><p>Darger died April 13, 1973, leaving behind a one-room Lincoln Park apartment at 851 W. Webster Ave., crammed with broken furniture, old record players and other debris he’d plucked from garbage cans. But beneath the trash, lay an extraordinary trove of his life’s work: hundreds of watercolors, collage paintings and, in a trunk, a 15,000-page typed fantasy novel titled “In the Realms of the Unreal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-470000" name="image-470000"></a> <picture Webster Ave. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Darger never married. He had no children. He was an unknown artist in his lifetime. His landlords, Nathan and Kiyoko Lerner, took possession of Darger’s works after, in failing health, he moved out of the apartment and into a Catholic nursing home. Kiyoko Lerner, who now lives in Japan, has testified that Darger told her husband that he no longer wanted his art and that Nathan Lerner could have it.</p><p>That artwork is now worth millions. Darger is considered among the world’s greatest “outsider” or self-taught artists. Over several decades, Kiyoko Lerner (Nathan Lerner died in 1997) has sold, reproduced, donated, exhibited and licensed countless Darger works, including selling at least 22 pieces to the American Folk Art Museum in New York for a total of $1 million in 2000.</p><p>The Art Institute of Chicago, the Intuit Art Museum and the Museum of Modern Art in New York all own Darger pieces.</p><p>But Darger left no written will. And so in 2022, a group of people claiming to be distant Darger relatives filed suit in federal court, arguing, among other things, that they are the rightful owners of Darger’s works, trademarks and numerous copyrights.</p><p>One of the potential heirs, Kristin Klein, spoke to the Sun-Times shortly after the federal suit was filed in 2022. Klein was living in Connecticut at the time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3f0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Works by Chicago artist Henry Darger, courtesy of Robert A. Roth, displayed at Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art in 2008. The mixed media creations are titled “Cat Headed Blengian,” left, and “Spangled Winged Tuskorhorian Blengin.” The reclusive writer-artist died in 1973 at age 81. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Charles Rex Arbogast/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I kind of think that us being relatives, yeah, we deserve part of his estate,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2022/2/22/22945676/henry-darger-artist-writer-books-apartment-contents-estate-court-battle-relatives-lincoln-park" target="_blank" ><u>Klein said in 2022.</u></a> “Just because we weren’t around when he was alive doesn’t mean that people who weren’t related to him deserve to have his entire estate. It should have gone to family to begin with.”</p><p>Darger’s state of mind in his declining years will likely come into play during the trial. Alan Jay Mandel, an attorney for the would-be heirs, told Judge Durkin Thursday that he is considering having a mental-health expert testify at trial.</p><p>In pre-trial court filings, attorneys for the potential heirs point to, among other things, Darger’s death certificate, which lists “senility” as a cause of death. Durkin has said in a written ruling in the case that the senility diagnosis is relevant, but that “the certificate does not establish as a matter of law that Darger lacked the capacity to make a gift.”</p><p>The trial will certainly attract attention from across the artworld, particularly among representatives of art galleries and museums that have Darger pieces in their collections.</p><p>One person who won’t be there is Ron Slattery, who died earlier this year.</p><p>Originally from Chicago, Slattery was a vintage photography collector. He and his wife, Fawn Slattery, were the ones who originally tracked down a potential Darger relative in 2019 to alert her to her possible claim to Darger's art and writings.</p><p>The Slatterys told the Sun-Times back in 2022 that they had never met the Lerners but felt the former landlords shouldn’t profit from Darger’s talent. The Lerners’ supporters have said that Darger would likely have remained unknown without the Lerners’ help in preserving and putting his artwork and writings out into the world.</p>

entries.title: Bears lose TE Cole Kmet for the season with knee injury
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' worst fears were confirmed Friday morning when testing showed tight end Cole Kmet will miss the rest of the season with a right knee injury.</p><p>“He's going to be sorely missed,” coach Ben Johnson said. “Really, he's Chicago. He's been here his whole life and he's a big part of our heartbeat. So it stinks. It does.<br>“I hate it for him, I hate it for his teammates as well.”</p><p>Kmet hurt his knee late in the fourth quarter of Thursday night’s 30-24 win against the Patriots after catching a nine-yard pass along the Bears' sideline. Shocked teammates gathered around him before he was carted to the locker room.</p><p>The 27-year-old tight end was drafted in 2020 in the same second round as teammate Jaylon Johnson. He’s signed through next year, carrying a $15.4 million salary cap hit against just a $5.4 million dead cap charge.</p><p>Kmet had 10 catches for 87 yards this season but was part of the league’s best rushing attack as the Bears’ most reliable blocking tight end.</p><p>"I don't have the words to describe what Cole is to me, what Cole is to this team, this organization," quarterback Caleb Williams said Thursday night. "He's the longest-tenured Bear, I believe. And so, he's been through it. And it's challenging. He's tough. And I'll be with him. I'll be right there with him through every step of whatever the injury is. Cole's been there for me every step of the way. Through the first year, the second year and now through this year. So, I can only do the same for him.”</p><p>Ben Johnson is among the league leaders in using multiple tight ends on the same play and figures to keep doing the same. Rookie third-round pick Sam Roush’s playing time will increase —“We’ve been very pleased with the improvement that he’s made,” Johnson said — and the Bears figure to promote either Stephen Carlson or Qadir Ismail from the practice squad. Johnson offered up a more unconventional option, too — using swing tackle Ozzy Trapilo as the third tight end in “Jumbo” packages.</p><p>“[Kmet] was consistently one of the highest-graded players on our offense, week-in and week-out,” Johnson said. “He will be missed, there’s no question about it. But in terms of what we do, it’s not gonna change a whole lot. ...</p><p>"The train keeps rolling along. Someone else has to step up."</p><h3>Sweat back</h3><h3></h3><p>The roster spot the Bears opened up by putting Kmet on injured reserve Friday was filled by defensive end Montez Sweat, who returned from a two-game drug suspension that was consistent with testing positive for diuretics or other performance-enhancing drug-masking agents.</p><p>The Bears had seven sacks in Sweat’s absence after posting 11 in five games with him.</p>

entries.title: Ann Tighe, attorney who was a finalist in consideration to be city's top federal prosecutor, dies at 87
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Ann C. Tighe's bid to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois did not result in her becoming the first woman to do the job. </p><p>It did result in a fresh conversation about the dynamics of power couples, gender roles, sacrifice and fair play.</p><p>Ms. Tighe (pronounced like the word "tie") was in private practice in 1997 when she was put on the shortlist of names being considered for the job — a high-profile law enforcement seat whose occupants have historically run point on investigations targeting a range of bad actors, including mafia figures and corrupt politicians. </p><p>But the fact that Ms. Tighe's husband, Jim Houlihan, was serving as Cook County Assessor at the time was seen by some as a potential conflict of interest.</p><p>To satisfy critics, including the Chicago Council of Lawyers, the Better Government Association and the media, Houlihan would have had to resign as assessor.</p><p>"I gave it serious thought," Houlihan told the Sun-Times when the couple sat for an interview in 1998. "I knew Ann was qualified for the job."</p><p>"I said to Jim, 'Don't you dare,'" Ms. Tighe said, adding that the measure would have been "a drastic step that was totally, completely unnecessary."</p><p>"I found it kind of insulting," said Houlihan. "The implication was that I'd be part of corruption."</p><p>Ms. Tighe had served as an assistant federal prosecutor in Chicago from 1974 to 1980, one of the first female attorneys to work in the office that she later sought to lead. </p><p>Even those who pointed out the potential conflict of interest did so without questioning Ms. Tighe's qualifications, her integrity or that of her husband. </p><p>Attorney Scott Lassar was ultimately named to the position in 1997, which has still never been held by a woman.</p><p>"I don't think the fact that I'm married to Jim should disqualify me. I think the fact that we've been married almost 25 years shows maturity and dedication," Ms. Tighe said in the interview with the Sun-Times shortly after learning she didn't get the gig.</p><p>"There are ways of dealing with any potential conflict that I felt totally comfortable with, and we both knew we would act appropriately. Obviously if there had been any investigation involving the assessor's office, I'd step aside," Tighe said.</p><p>For Ms. Tighe, who had to get permission from a judge in 1973 to practice law under her own name, not her husband's name, "the thought of being the first woman [U.S. attorney] was very exciting. It is a very powerful office. I just thought it would be good for women."</p><p>Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) at the time accused Ms. Tighe's critics of being "trapped in an ancient mindset."</p><p>Ms. Tighe died Tuesday from natural causes. She was 87.</p><p>"In today's norms that conflict of interest would be laughable, but that was then, this is now," said friend and lobbyist Tom Murphy.</p><p>The episode may have stung, but it did not diminish her career.</p><p>For decades she worked as a white-collar criminal defense attorney and became a named partner in the firm now known as Cotsirilos, Poulos & Campbell. </p><p>"Ann was the first lady of the white-collar criminal defense," said former colleague Theodore Poulos.</p><p>"And she had this unique sounding laugh that everybody just adored," Poulos said. "She was joyous and classy, but tough as nails and did not suffer fools."</p><p>Ms. Tighe, who figure skated while growing up in Highland Park, kept a pair of skates in her Loop law office and skated as often as she could during her lunch breaks at an ice rink at Block 37.</p><p>She loved spending time at her family's summer home in Beverly Shores, Indiana. </p><p>Ms. Tighe, who practiced law into her 80s, graduated from Stanford University and attended law school at Northwestern University.</p><p>Ms. Tighe faced gender discrimination early in her career, beginning with a male professor who, when asked to write a letter to help her get into law school, responded: "Why would I help you get a spot that would otherwise be held for a man to help him get a job and feed his family?" her husband, Jim Houlihan, said this week.</p><p>"She went on to be a star," he said.</p><p>In addition to her husband, Ms. Tighe is survived by her sons Mike Houlihan and Daniel Houlihan, as well as five grandchildren.</p><p>A visitation will be held at at Old St. Patrick's Church on Tuesday, Oct. 27, from 2:30 to 4:30 p.m. with a funeral Mass immediately after.</p>

entries.title: CPS high school graduation and college enrollment rates rise, but many students still struggle to finish
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools students are increasingly earning college credits while still in high school and are graduating and enrolling in college at higher rates than in the past, but many still struggle to finish college and earn a degree.</p><p>Those are among the findings of a <a class="Link" href="https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/pai/2025/#" target="_blank" ><u>report released Friday</u></a> by the To&Through Project and the UChicago Consortium on School Research, coupled with district data released earlier this week.</p><p>The report found that 56% of CPS students who graduated in the class of 2019 and immediately enrolled in a four-year college got their degree or a workforce certificate within six years, while 32% of those who immediately began at a two-year institution earned a degree or certificate within the same time period. Those percentages have barely budged for four years.</p><p>Overall, only 48% of 2019 CPS graduates who immediately enrolled in college earned a degree or certificate within six years, the report found — far below the 64% national rate.</p><p>At the same time, CPS students are graduating and enrolling in college at or near all-time high rates. CPS’ graduation rate rose to 82.6% for the class of 2025, and the graduation rate rose again for the class of 2026 to 83.4%, district officials said this week.</p><p>Meanwhile, 67% of the class of 2025 immediately enrolled in college, up from 58% a decade ago and above the national average, according to the report.</p><p>The data indicates that while more high schoolers are reaching the next level of their education, many still need additional resources and support once they get there.</p><p>But Dominique McKoy, executive director of the To&Through Project, added that it also shows how far graduation rates have grown in recent decades.</p><p>“We got to remember that within living memory this was a district in the city that had a high school graduation rate of 50%,” he said. “We had some community areas in the city of Chicago with high school graduation rates of 25%.”</p><p>The report also found persistent racial and gender disparities within college completion rates.</p><p>Among 2019 CPS graduates, young men were much less likely to graduate with a college degree in six years than young women — a pattern that held true across every racial and ethnic group, according to the report. The disparity was especially stark for young Black and Latino men, with fewer than one-third of whom graduating with a bachelor’s degree within six years.</p><p>Young Latina women, Asian and Pacific Islanders and white students in the class of 2019 completed a degree or certificate at higher rates, the report found.</p><p>Mckoy said that the data provides “probably some of the strongest evidence around the necessity around initiatives” such as CPS’ Black Student Success Plan, which aims to reduce academic disparities among Black students.</p><p>The report notes that students who started college in 2019 and those that graduated high school in 2025 went through major events that affected their schooling, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign last year.</p><p>Still, overall college completion rates among CPS students have slowly increased over time.</p><p>The percentage of CPS graduates who enrolled in a four-year college and completed a degree of any kind within six years increased from around 53% to just under 56% from the class of 2010 to 2019. And that increase was even higher for those who enrolled in two-year colleges.</p><p>The district’s graduation rate has risen steadily over the past two decades. In 2000, less than half of CPS students graduated within four years, district data show. CPS reached its all-time high graduation rate in 2023, when nearly 85% of students got their diploma on time, according to the To&Through and UChicago report.</p><p>These students are earning college and workforce credentials during their high school years at a higher rate, too. More than 57% of CPS graduates in the class of 2026 earned college credits and career certificates, 10 percentage points higher than four years ago, according to district data released this week.</p><p>That includes technical certifications in skilled trades, credit for Advanced Placement courses and the seal of biliteracy, an award that recognizes students who demonstrate proficiency in English and another language, which can qualify for college credit.</p>

entries.title: Man critically wounded in afternoon North Lawndale shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was left in critical condition after he was shot in North Lawndale Friday afternoon, police said.</p><p>The 37-year-old man was near the sidewalk in the 3900 block of West Cermak Road around 3 p.m. when he was approached by an unknown person.</p><p>The person, armed with a firearm, fired multiple times at the man, officials said. </p><p>He was struck several times and was taken to the hospital in critical condition, Chicago police said.</p><p>Detectives are investigating.</p>
