entries.title: Salt Shed owners eye amphitheater expansion across from popular West Town venue
entries.summary: <p>The Salt Shed could soon see a sister venue across the street that would include an amphitheater, bar and outdoor plaza.</p><p>The expansion plans were outlined in a zoning application filed with the City Council on Oct. 14 by a limited liability company tied to the Salt Shed. </p><p>The plans note that Blue Star Properties and 16” on Center, the hospitality collective whose portfolio includes Empty Bottle, SPACE, Thalia Hall and the Salt Shed, don’t own the land where the expansion is proposed. But if a sale goes through, the plot at 1401-59 N. Magnolia Ave. would expand the companies’ entertainment holdings and the industrial-to-entertainment transformation happening along the North Branch of the Chicago River.</p><p>The companies didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Plans for Salt Shed's expansion first emerged in October 2025, when Crain's Chicago Business <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/commercial-real-estate/salt-shed-owners-eye-adjacent-property-big-expansion/" target="_blank" >reported</a> the venue's owners were targeting the empty parcels for an outdoor music venue. </p><p>The site span 516,316 square feet and hugs the east side of the Chicago River. The lots are sometimes used for parking during shows and other events at the Salt Shed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ed0000" name="image-ed0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d98dccb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5a%2F01%2F62fcf0104468839c48052b3e4d36%2Fsaltshed-261026-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e7ebc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5a%2F01%2F62fcf0104468839c48052b3e4d36%2Fsaltshed-261026-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4f0a985/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5a%2F01%2F62fcf0104468839c48052b3e4d36%2Fsaltshed-261026-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Aerial view of an empty lot at 1459 N. Magnolia Ave. across the street from Salt Shed is where the venue wants to expand, with an outdoor amphitheater along the North Branch of the Chicago River in Chicago on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Mark Black/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Site plans show a parking lot along West Le Moyne Street, with roughly 100 spaces for attendees and artists. Next to the lot would be offices and a building with artist dressing rooms, and the rest of the site, near West Blackhawk Street, would have an amphitheater and seating. There would also be a VIP seating section close to the stage, flanked by a general admission standing area and tiered seating behind it. In the center, behind VIP seating, is a bar.</p><p>West Blackhawk Street — which separates the Salt Shed and the prospective amphitheater — would be transformed into a landscaped public plaza connecting the two venues. Plans also show a pedestrian bridge on a portion of the street that would connect the venues. West Blackhawk Street is already closed during shows for security and entry lines.</p><p>The expansion would be a huge boon for the Salt Shed’s owners. The former Morton Salt factory venue is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/03/chicago-indie-venues-health-metro-ramova-salt-shed" >selling out most shows</a>, the Sun-Times and WBEZ previously reported, and leaning into an on-site music village concept with a record store, guitar shop and food trucks. Earlier this year, tattoo parlor Deluxe Tattoo opened an outpost at the Salt Shed, offering tattoos inspired by artists performing at the venue.</p><p>The Salt Shed has a capacity of roughly 5,500 people for outdoor shows and 3,600 for indoor shows. The site plan doesn't specify the capacity of the new amphitheater, though Crain's Chicago Business previously reported it could be up to 15,000. </p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson on failed trick play: 'Shooters shoot. ... We missed'
entries.summary: <p>Coach Ben Johnson didn’t back down from his decision to hand the ball off to guard Joe Thuney on Thursday against the Patriots, even as he acknowledged the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> were flagged because they did it the wrong way.</p><p>‘‘It’s one of those things where shooters shoot,’’ he said Friday. ‘‘We shot, we missed. Keep it moving.’’</p><p>The Bears were flagged for an illegal forward handoff after quarterback Caleb Williams handed the ball forward to Thuney after faking a handoff to running back D’Andre Swift, who had lined up in the left slot and was running right.</p><p>The rules say a team only can hand the ball off backward to an ineligible receiver. The last time a team was flagged for the violation was the Lions 16 years ago. Thuney had to be behind Williams to take the handoff, Johnson said.</p><p>‘‘It’s got to be backwards, it’s as simple as that,’’ Johnson said.</p><p>The Bears installed the play weeks ago, Johnson said. At first, he had Williams put the ball on the ground for Thuney to pick up.</p><p>‘‘Which, in hindsight, might have been the way to go,’’ Johnson said.</p><p>Williams said after the game he didn’t know the rule existed. Thuney said the play ‘‘was fun but illegal, I guess.’’</p>

entries.title: DOJ allowed to join lawsuit against Evanston reparations program for Black residents
entries.summary: <p>The Department of Justice is officially allowed to join a lawsuit against Evanston’s historic yet highly contested reparations program after a judge approved the agency’s motion last week, according to court records.</p><p>District Judge John F. Kness approved the DOJ’s motion to join <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suburban-chicago/2024/05/29/evanstons-reparations-program-violates-equal-protection-us-constitution-lawsuit-claims-civil-rights" >a 2024 class-action legal challenge from Judicial Watch</a>, a conservative nonprofit, against the City of Evanston's reparations program, which launched in 2021 with the stated goal of remediating past racial housing discrimination of Black residents between 1919 and 1969.</p><p>Joining six residents who are not Black but say their relatives lived in Evanston during the 50-year reparation qualification period, the DOJ claims the program violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Fair Housing Act.</p><p>“Evanston has chosen to distribute substantial benefits to persons solely because of their race or the race of their ancestors,” the federal government’s motion states. “The Program does not provide any opportunities for compensation for residents of other races who may have lived in the area where black residents were segregated and suffered adverse housing consequences as a result.”</p><p>The first U.S. city to fund a local reparations program, Evanston <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/3/22/22345860/evanston-passes-first-in-nation-reparations" >officially approved</a> its program in 2021.</p><p>Nearly five years later, the Justice Department announced in June its intention to join the <i>Flinn, et al. v. City of Evanston</i> lawsuit and now has the necessary approval to move forward with its plan.</p><p>“This is an effort to intimidate,” former Evanston mayor Daniel Biss <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/in-the-loop-with-sasha-ann-simons/2026/07/01/architects-of-evanston-reparations-program-stand-firm-against-doj-attacks" target="_blank" >told WBEZ</a> in July after the DOJ announced its plan to join the lawsuit. “This is an effort by the Trump administration to tell anyone who’s interested, ‘back off, we’re going to come for you.’”</p><p>Evanston’s first reparations policies offered a maximum of $25,000 in housing grants to Black people who lived in the city or had ancestors who lived in the city during the 50-year period of racially discriminatory housing policies. In 2023, Evanston amended its policy to offer eligible applicants unrestricted cash payments, rather than requiring the $25,000 to go toward housing subsidies.</p><p>The DOJ’s brief emphasized that Evanston no longer requires beneficiaries “to provide any account of how they use the funds.”</p><p>The Evanston accepted reparation applications for 45 days in 2021 and has not accepted any applications since November 5 of that year, according to the DOJ. In a 2024 motion to dismiss the case, the City of Evanston stated it “does not have any current plans to reopen applications.”</p><p>Evanston paid 141 applicants who qualified as an “Ancestor” and has begun paying 454 others who qualified as “Direct Descendants,” totaling more than $5 million worth of reparation, according to the DOJ.</p><p>In its lawsuit, the DOJ acknowledges instances in which race can be used when “remediating specific, identified instances of past discrimination that violated the Constitution or a statute.” But the Department details that Evanston’s program is too general and does not identify a specific scope of past discrimination the city intends to correct.</p><p>“The City’s racially discriminatory program is not narrowly tailored to remedy specific identified instances of past discrimination,” the brief states. “They contain virtually no information about what the alleged discriminatory acts or policies were, during what years the discriminatory acts occurred, the policies that were in effect, or the scope of the injury caused by these acts or policies.”</p><p>Biss, who ended his second mayoral term on Sunday and is running to represent Illinois' 9th congressional district in Congress, has been at the forefront of the reparations program since its founding. During his July interview, he rejected the claim that Evanston’s program is not specific in its eligibility requirements or intended goals.</p><p>“The city dug deep in our history. We worked with scholars to understand what we’ve done. We documented real harm that not only happened in the past but is being felt right now by residents of Evanston," the then-Evanston-mayor told WBEZ.</p><p>Evanston motioned for the case to be thrown out in July 2024, stating that the six complainants had not proven they were “ready” and eligible to apply for the grants during the time the program was accepting applications, notwithstanding their racial identities.</p>

entries.title: College football second-half preview and Week 8 predictions
entries.summary: <p>Before we get to my Week 8 picks, let’s catch up on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >college football</a> season at roughly the midway point and look ahead to the second half. Ten things you need to know about the final season before an expanded, 24-team playoff likely kicks in next year:</p><p><b>1. College Football Playoff rankings: </b>The committee’s initial rankings will be unveiled Tuesday, Nov. 3, meaning familiar refrains such as “ESPN is killing the sport,” “the SEC and Big Ten are megalomaniacal terrorists” and “Oh, please, Notre Dame hasn’t beaten anybody” are right around the corner.</p><p><b>2. All the unbeatens: </b>Wait, did somebody say “all”? Last year at this point, there were 10 of them. This time, we’re at only five after Georgia, Notre Dame and Indiana all got dinged in Week 7 and James Madison went down on Thursday. Miami, BYU, Texas Tech, Utah and UCLA still haven’t lost.</p><p><b>3. Irish stew: </b>After being left out of the 12-team playoff last year at 10-2, Notre Dame is back in the thick of trouble, needing to finish 5-0 to avoid high drama and a potential recurrence of outrage on selection day. A Nov. 7 date with Miami in South Bend will come with massive pressure on Marcus Freeman’s team.</p><p><b>4. Big Tension: </b>A year ago this week in the Top 25, unbeaten Ohio State was ranked No. 1, unbeaten Indiana was No. 2 and one-loss Oregon was No. 6. Now, one-loss OSU is at 3, one-loss Indiana at 6 and perfect UCLA at 9. Producing another national champion — what would be a fourth straight for the conference — is going to take some seriously heavy lifting.</p><p><b>5. North by Northwestern: </b>At 5-1 and with a sparkling new stadium, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/17/northwestern-wildcats-michigan-state-spartans-pat-fitzgerald-aidan-chiles-david-braun" target="_blank" >the Wildcats are having a moment</a>. With games to go at Oregon, against Iowa and at Ohio State, though, among other losable ones, the rest of the season might be pretty rough. Meanwhile, the school is already offering discounted tickets to faculty and staff just to try to fill the 35,000-seat joint.</p><p><b>6. I-L-L … spells “ill”: </b>After 19 wins over the last two seasons, Illinois is 3-3 and likely will be the underdog in at least four of its remaining games. A bowl? Maybe, maybe not. Basketball season? It can’t ever start soon enough.</p><p><b>7. The coaching carousel: </b>Maryland fired Mike Locksley this week, making him the first coach to get the ax — six fewer than had been jettisoned by this time last season. On hot seats from here are, among many others, Rutgers’ Greg Schiano, Florida State’s Mike Norvell, Wisconsin’s Luke Fickell, USC’s Lincoln Riley and possibly Colorado’s Deion Sanders.</p><p><b>8. First-half Heisman: </b>My all-important vote for this nonexistent award goes to Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith. Already with 52 catches for 984 yards and 12 touchdowns, the best player in the country is the clear frontrunner.</p><p><b>9. End-of-season Heisman: </b>It’s a quarterback award, after all, isn’t it? That gives No. 1-ranked Miami’s QB, Darian Mensah, who has 18 TD passes and only one interception and owns the best passer rating in the land, a real shot. In one order or the other, Smith and Mensah will be the top two.</p><p><b>10. Games of the second half: </b>Miami at Notre Dame (Week 10), BYU at Utah (Week 10), Georgia at Ole Miss (Week 10), Texas at LSU (Week 11), Michigan at Ohio State (Week 13), USC at UCLA (Week 13).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-470000" name="image-470000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a14288b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ff1dabb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Northwestern quarterback Aidan Chiles makes a call at the line during a game against Ball State in Evanston on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/04eb328/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Northwestern quarterback Aidan Chiles makes a call at the line during a game against Ball State in Evanston on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Melisssa Tamez/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Week 8 picks</b></h3><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>No. 24 Northwestern (-15½) vs. Rutgers </b>(11 a.m., Peacock, 720-AM): I’m no expert in stadium promotions, but maybe Northwestern should let the first 10,000 fans get into the game and make a handoff against the Scarlet Knights, owners of the second-worst rushing defense among all Power 4 teams. Wildcats, 38-24.</p><p><b>No. 6 Indiana (-7½) at Michigan </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): Imagine giving an eight-figure NIL deal to a quarterback and then having to bench him in his second season because he just seems to make the offense worse. That seems to be where the Wolverines are at with Bryce Underwood. What a tough ask of freshman Tommy Carr — brother of former Notre Dame QB CJ and grandson of U-M icon Lloyd Carr — if he gets the start against a defense as salty as Indiana’s. Hoosiers, 21-13.</p><p><b>No. 15 Iowa (-7½) at Minnesota </b>(2:30 p.m., FS1): The Gophers have a huge Iowa problem, having lost 10 of the last 11 and 20 of the last 25 against the Hawkeyes, including blowouts each of the last two seasons. Just paint Floyd of Rosedale black and gold already and get it over with. Hawkeyes, 27-20.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 19 Texas (-3½) vs. No. 7 Ole Miss </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): As good as he is, Longhorns QB Arch Manning just can’t stop making mistakes. Speaking of the Heisman, Ole Miss QB Trinidad Chambliss could put himself right in the race with one of his A-Game performances and an upset. The better defense wears burnt orange, though, and it’s not close.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Illinois (+9½) vs. Oregon </b>(2 p.m., BTN, 890-AM): If the Ducks who went to USC and won by 14 show up to Memorial Stadium, I’ll be wrong. Overall, though, they haven’t been this un-scary since the Mario Cristobal years. Run the ball? They haven’t been able to do it. Stop the pass? Same. The Illini have a legit upset shot — take the points.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>4-3 straight-up, 6-1 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>37-14 straight-up, 28-23 against the spread.</p>

entries.title: 'Fearless' Humboldt penguin joins colony at Brookfield Zoo
entries.summary: <p>A “fearless” young Humboldt penguin has officially entered the habitat.</p><p>Robin, a female juvenile penguin, is the only Humboldt penguin to hatch at the Brookfield Zoo this year. She hatched July 7 to first-time parents Sofi and Klaus.</p><p>“She's a tenacious little girl,” said Amanda Mansfield, senior animal care specialist at the zoo. “She's going to be a wonderful ambassador for her wild counterparts.”</p><p>Robin was moved as an egg and placed with foster parents Cara and Popero, who have successfully raised chicks in the past, according to Mansfield. She spent her first three weeks under their care before zoo experts stepped in to help raise her.</p><p>But Robin is different from other chicks, said Mansfield.</p><p>Penguin chicks are born covered in down feathers that make swimming difficult for the first few months. But Robin showed an interest in getting into the water at a very young age.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a swimming through the Humboldt penguin habitat Friday morning.</p><p>Robin joined the colony last week and is still learning to make friends, said Mansfield.</p><p>“Her job right now is to find her place where she's comfortable and how to interact and communicate with the other penguins,” she said. “She’s doing really well.”</p><p>She was poked by a couple of the older penguins, but Mansfield said that was “normal penguin communication.”</p><p>Brookfield Zoo is home to 24 Humboldt penguins, a species native to the rocky Pacific coast and offshore islands of Peru and Chile.</p><p>The zoo
